records.title: Show HN: Ultimidi – piano learning web game
records.author: XCSme
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

10 years ago, as my BsC final project I had the idea to make a quick game that used neural nets to detect notes played on a guitar, and I made a small mini-game to make use of that. I always wanted to improve on that idea, so last year I started making my own piano-learning game.

You know how in most games you learn complex key combinations and sequences (i.e. Mortal Kombat fatalities), but those don't have much use outside of the game.

My idea was to make a game that can be played with the piano, so you you learn notes, chords, scales simply by playing.

While making it and prototyping many versions, I realised that that idea didn't work as well as I wanted, because it is hard to focus on reading notes, playing and some other gameplay logic.

In the end I settled on a combination of basic beat-based notes playing and a few minigames that use the piano as input. My goal now is to add even more such minigames, for learning different sheet reading, music theory and piano playing techniques.

For art, I am unfortunately not a designer and have no budget for hiring one, so I decided to go with some simple shaped art generated in bulk using AI rendering SVGs. Hopefully this is just a placeholder until I find someone to do the art for the game.

You can try it out for free, it does have some extra content in the Pro version, but a lotof content is free, including the ability to directly play full songs in scrolling or sheet mode here: https://game.ultimidi.com/songs

Happy to hear any feedback, especially if the MIDI connection/notes detection didn't work or something doesn't feel good.

Thank you!

records.title: Show HN: UIPalooza – Do AI models have a recognizable design taste?
records.author: joeysim
records.storyText:
This question has been bugging me for a while: do different AI models have a different design sense? Does it matter which one I pick?

I built UI Palooza to explore that. I gave models the same four frontend briefs, with enough room to choose their own typography, colors, layouts, and interactions. Then I repeated the runs with different design skills and sample directions.

The public collection has 1,784 designs. You can compare them side by side and open the working websites, not just screenshots. No signup required.

One way to explore it: pick a brief and Baseline A, then compare Vanilla with a design skill. Or keep the skill fixed and look across models.

I’d be interested in which patterns you notice—and what you’d change about the experiment.

records.title: Show HN: A 3D mesh playground for coding agents (three.js + manifold-3d)
records.author: wsxiaoys
records.storyText:
When GPT-6/Gemini launched recently, a lot of the 3D demos used blender-mcp (https://github.com/ahujasid/blender-mcp). It's cool, but you have to install blender locally and wire up plugins just to try a prompt or share a run.

I built a browser-based 3D mesh playground so you can hook up your own coding agent over MCP (or run in-browser) directly in a tab. It runs on three.js + manifold-3d for blender-like boolean/mesh editing in JS, and gives the agent a render_preview tool to take multi-view screenshots (front/right/top/iso + custom camera angles + clay mode). That way the agent can look at what it built and fix the geometry, similar to how it iterates when building a website.

The submitted link is a trace of Gemini reconstructing a Copenhagen canal scene from a photo: it hits a script error on the first pass, fixes the bug, and then goes through several rounds of checking 4-view and close-up render_preview screenshots to tweak the geometry.

records.title: Show HN: I built Search/Recsys that learns from feedback
records.author: bicsi
records.storyText:
Hi HN. A while ago I started building a generic people matching app based on LLM-as-a-judge. I needed a way to bypass the O(n^2) "everyone rates everyone else" trap, but generic RAG was much worse than expected.

DNA is a search-like API at the core of that product. It stores one embedding per item (like a vector DB) and gives the best match(es). You evaluate them in some way (LLM / Decision Model / users), and send the score back. This makes it improve in real time, so next time it gives you better results. In my tests, it needed 7x fewer LLM judgments than scoring down the embedding list. Paper in progress.

What I don’t know yet is what demo would make you want to try building with it. What would you want to see it do?

records.title: Show HN: Nodecode, open-source living agent in Lisp that rewrites itself for you
records.author: svsairevanth
records.storyText:
Hi HN, we're Mike and Thom.

Agents of the future should only have one tool (the interpreter, ideally a LISP eval), nothing more or less; to interact with the world. Agents remember by writing markdown files. NODECODE remembers by rewriting itself. And that is in itself a new paradigm in working with agents. What if memories, skills, MCPs, provider connectors, tools, etc. all live under the same image as *.lisp files instead of in disarray across random folders?

Ask it for something it can’t do, and it writes what it needs into its OWN running image and keeps it even after a restart. (Changes in a LISP image have significantly lower ceremony and overhead than in harnesses written in other languages):

Small intuitive scenario:

> you can't read PDFs. teach yourself. (defun read-pdf (path) ...) ; runs at once, kept (read-pdf "invoices/0421.pdf") ;; Globex owes $1,240.00, due Oct 24, unpaid. [… rest of PDF content]

read-pdf is still there after a restart, in your terminal, and in every other UI clients (Discord, web app, etc.)

Technically at a lower level; NODECODE runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates LISP in the running program. Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. What the model defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start.

Why LISP now? Current SOTA models have reached an optimum point in how they efficiently work with LISP, though not as fluently as Python. Still, we believe AGI will understand ANY language (past/present/future) by understanding the crux of any given language, and not through excessive and expensive pretraining scheme.

Why LISP in general? We believe LISP is the current language that communicates to the world with the least bandwidth.

Why another LISP agent? The LISP harnesses we found are hard to use unless you already know the language itself, and so we had this idea of simplifying and condensing the UX to be user friendly for the masses, while leveraging the power of LISP. Code as data is what lets an agent change itself, and that shouldn't need a LISP hacker to run. NODECODE is our first step toward putting it on everyone's PC and mobile. You ask in plain words, the model writes LISP, and you get briefed in natural language; that is how it should be.

Extensions? Code as data also suits extensions. We see NODECODE as a living agent organism. To us, it feels very much alive, and so this brings us to the Cells system. A Cell is a folder that teaches NODECODE something new: a chat room it can live in (e.g Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc. - Yes we made Cells for channels to have it act as a very capable personal agent), a skill, a memory, MCPs, new tools, etc. Install one from our Cell hub or ask it to write a custom, personalized one. Either way it is more code the agent can read and change.

Your terminal, a browser tab, your phone and bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack all attach to that SAME gateway process, so a tool it writes in one is there in ALL of them. Over time it becomes yours and it is continuously evolving; the organism within it; NODECODE.

MIT License. https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode X/twitter/demo launch post: https://x.com/pomterree/status/2113721985167728757 docs: https://nodecode.ai/docs

records.title: Show HN: Radian, an agent puts development workflow on autopilot
records.author: anylut
records.storyText:
I have built an indie hacker project; my main flow was:

1. chatting with Claud Code about the general plan

2. assigning slices of work to other worker agents like Pi + DeepSeek 4.1 Flash

3. building in parallel

4. Claud Code reviews when done, runs tests, and merges after I validate

It worked, but with a lot of glue in the middle, so I built radian + arc into the same binary.

Radian: a compact, pragmatic agent that has enough tooling to solve a small coding task end to end; it does not try to be a plugin platform. You can still extend it via MCP, skills, or hooks to extend its capabilities. I think plugins are great, but a lot of them are for humans. I'm trying to remove humans from the loop. Humans are at the start and end of the loop.

arc: built into the radian binary;

* it can get work sent from another agent

* assign work items to concurrent headless radian agents

* automatically review, CICD, integrate locally

* humans can still be in the loop but not at the agent conversation or code review level, but at the work item approval/review level.

* shows all of the above in a plan view or Kanban board in TUI.

I have been heavily dogfooding, and Radian + arc basically built themselves in the last couple of weeks, with me just being a product manager/scrum master and qa.

radian + arc are open source at https://github.com/hisea/radian

What do you think about this approach? Looking for ideas to make Radian better or fit more scenarios.

records.title: Show HN: Render your Windows desktop GUI on the NPU
records.author: jackwsmth
records.storyText:
Hi HN, a kind of funny project we've been hacking on for a couple of weeks.

We wanted to see if it was possible to get Windows into using the NPU like a GPU, and compositing the desktop GUI.

Why?

Well the longer-term idea is to free up the GPU as much as possible so eventually, you could have more GPU free for AI inference.

By offloading the work to the NPU we did manage to bring 3D GPU usage down from 3.4% to 0.6%... but at a large expense to performance (you will get 1.6 FPS doing this).

All of this was tested on an Intel NPU on a Panther Lake machine.

Check it out and let me know your thoughts!

records.title: Show HN: Deepswapp Browser: browser the browser with another browser

records.storyText:
A "deepswapp" of a website has data from one website in a layout of another website. Deepswapp Browser allows users to seamlessly browse this alternative version of the Internet, today.

Video: https://deepswapp.com/assets/deepswapp.mp4

The whole Web can look like Wikipedia, old Reddit, or your own website. Once deepswapped, the website transformation is reusable without AI.

    Single-file HTML page
    Only essential data rendered
    Synchronized tabs
    Synchronized scrolling
    No backgrounds
    No animations
    Data auto-refresh
    Image lazy loading
This desktop app works on every platform (Docker images also available) and opens a separate Chrome instance, which mirrors opened tabs in the user's main browser. Several deepswapps are included with the download, so no AI subscription is needed for a test drive. A fresh deepswapp takes around 10 minutes and costs about $0.40c on deepseek-v4.1-flash. This goes down by half when deepswapping a known website.

Tech side: fully in Golang, with AI-generated JavaScript never executing in the user's main browser.

Roadmap: Web and Mobile access, even deeper swaps, parallel swaps.

records.title: Show HN: Comparing SF Bay Area trash rates
records.author: shasheene
records.storyText:
I created this webpage to compare the rates for trash hauling across the San Francisco Bay Area.

I wanted to see how Oakland California compares to the rest of the region. I knew the rates were high, but I wanted to quantify how high. Especially since the cost of proper trash disposal contributes substantially to Oakland's illegal dumping problem.

I found some interesting insights between wealthiest cities on the peninsula and Oakland, because a city like Atherton actually pays substantially less than Oakland for 20 gallon trash service. I would have expected the operational expenditure related to service delivery to be lower in Oakland, so rates would be lower.

Also, trash hauling has some well-publicized cases of corruption (including the current federal indictment aginst former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao involving waste collection executives).

I think the transparency provided by a webpage like this can only be a good thing.

Please let me know what you think and any feedback.

records.title: Show HN: A Blender addon that makes Claude twice as efficient at using nodes
records.author: carson-katri
records.storyText:
I originally made this addon 4 years ago, but recently discovered that coding agents love it.

The addon adds a scripting API for Blender’s node trees, such as Geometry Nodes or Shader Nodes.

It generates a function and related types for every node in Blender. Then the agent (or you) can write scripts to create node trees without having to guess what the node, input, and output names are.

It’s meant to be used alongside the Blender MCP.

In my tests, Opus finishes building node trees in at least half the time using at least half the tokens to answer the same prompt.

Because the scripting API forces it to build correct node trees, it has to back track less to fix mistakes. This saves a lot of time and tokens. There is also a skill and some helper functions to let it look up the function signatures for nodes.

Let me know how it works for you!

records.title: Show HN: git-dupe – Version private files alongside a public Git repo
records.author: WayHow
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I made git-dupe to solve the problem where I have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of my personal workflow, so I do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, I want them to be in the project at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because I want versioning for them.

The solution that I've come upon is versioning those agent files in another repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to me and holds the history for my agent files). The project itself is open to the public in another <public-repo>. I overlap the two repos to solve the problem (i.e., they share the same worktree).

  $ git status --short              # the public repo
  ?? AGENTS.md
  ?? notes/

  $ git dupe init                   # the private repo
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/

  $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md   # the private repo
  hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it

  $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions"        # the private repo
  [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions
   3 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
   create mode 100644 .gitdupe
   create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
   create mode 100644 notes/todo.md

  $ git status --short              # the public repo: nothing

  $ git dupe log --oneline          # the private repo: your files
  3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions
In short, git-dupe allows two Git repos to share the same worktree, while using native Git for most operations. Most git-dupe commands behave just like normal Git commands, operating on the private repo instead.

git-dupe currently supports Linux and macOS, and is under the MIT License; the git-dupe repo contains much more extensive technical documentation documentation for those who are interested. If you have any feedback/questions about git-dupe, feel free to message. I hope it helps!

Fun fact: the git-dupe project itself is using git-dupe for versioning.

It’s a single static binary that does one thing, aiming to avoid the large surface area and security issues that have plagued some LLM gateways.

Traffic is distributed by LLM provider latency and availability. The share going to other providers acts as a probe, so that a recovered provider wins back traffic automatically.

records.title: Show HN: Building the European Company Graph one website at a time
records.author: leo_researchly
records.storyText:
At Researchly (https://www.researchly.at) we automate market and competitive analysis. We learned that on-the-fly web search through AI agents isn't reliable enough for consistent, in-depth work.

Existing data providers such as PitchBook or Crunchbase are either too expensive or lack the data we need: operational signals such as management changes or new partnerships, for DACH. Furthermore, search tools such as Exa tend to be probabilistic. What they return depends on the model and on SEO rankings, so two runs of the same query can give you two different answers.

So we built our own search layer: several providers (Exa, Linkup, Tavily, Parallel), allow/deny lists, source rankings (we once caught ourselves citing our own blog posts), and checks whether an empty result means "nothing there" or "out of budget".

It works, but: it's slow, expensive, non-deterministic & we kept redoing the same research for different clients (which makes it very un-economic).

So we started building the data layer itself. Step one was Firmendaten (300k companies from the Austrian register; shared here last week https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50142669).

Relational data like that is already a huge improvement, but what we really need is a graph, as people ask "W" questions: who does what with whom where and when. This is our first attempt at it.

For now, it just connects who partners with whom and company groups. (Tick "Beziehungen 2. Ebene" to see every partner and person)

It's small (a few dozen robotics companies) but you can already see how complex the graph gets & it serves as a good PoC for us.

We had wanted to build this for a long time, and it turned out to be far harder than we expected. One thing that sounds trivial but was particularly hard: finding the right website for a company.

You can buy that data. There are enrichment APIs that return a company's website. But even if they cover Austrian companies, how do you know which company they matched? There is no worldwide unique company identifier.

And if you do it yourself: how do you know that this website really belongs to this company? You have to validate every single match (e. g. through the imprint on a company's website in Austria).

There are quite a few more challenges involved, but we're happy with where this first, admittedly small, result has landed. Feedback very welcome – especially on which relationships would make a graph like this useful for you.

Feedback welcome!

records.title: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share
records.author: arcanemachiner
records.storyText:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl

records.title: Show HN: Tabverse – a free, open-source, with self-hostable server Workona clone
records.author: liyu1981au
records.storyText:
Hi, I want to share with you my chrome extension: Tabverse, as it is now passed the reveiw of Chrome Web Store and live at: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabverse/lffblcippn...

Tabverse is a local first workona like chrome extension for managing tabs, with its source open at https://www.github.com/liyu1981/tabverse.

In essential it has the core functions workona has, but can operate totally locally, which means it will not need an account nor subscription. The only limit is your local storage spaces so that you can have as many spaces(I call tabverse) as you can. It is open source, so not just your data stays with you, and the tool itself will stay with you in future.

Beyond the normal workona features (persisted workspace, load/reload/import/export, note/bookmark/history tools), there are features does require a server. Features like backup/sync, global search on all tabverses, and future collaboration (not yet done), can only be possible if there is a server. I build this part in open too: the server is free to self host and open source in same repo of Tabverse.

The tabverse's idea was with me few years ago while I was using Workona and was frustrated with its limitation on free tier (remember was only 5 workspaces), and the missing features of managing multiple workspaces at the same time. Tabverse takes the idea of Workona, and develop further: each window with a Tabverse tab is a workspace, all stored in local storage, and multi windows can have multi Tabverses same time, and can switch fast. There can even be window without Tabverse, so besides work, personal stuff or entertainment will have place to go. As I build this alone, in the middle, almost give up on this project, and luckily AI agents now is there: not only I have a good helper, but also I have a partner I can discuss a bit. So this time the first version starts with v0.7.2.

But AI agent can never replace the real need from human on what should be built and what works better, so I want to share with you and listen to your feedbacks early. Please give it a try, and every feedback to me is a gift.

Besides the self-hosted option, I host a server at https://tabverse.liyu1981.xyz (yes, the same website of intro and docs), but is invitation only. If you want to help me to test in this early stage, you can login with Google (the only social login I configured :)), and request an invitation there. I will act as soon as I find your request :). But do not worry at all if you only want to use Tabverse locally without a server -- that is the first thing when I was building it.

In current version there are also AI features built in, and again do not worry as the AI features is using Chrome's Prompt API, which is totally local, with Gemini Nano (first time will need to download it automatically), nothing send to a server, and you can always turn this on of off in settings. Morden computers with decent memory should work well, but some older computer may suffer (so please turn off). And it is Chrome only. (Honestly, Tabverse currently only support Google Chrome, but not other Chrome based browsers).

records.title: Show HN: Optio – A self-hosted orchestration platform for AI agents
records.author: jawiggins
records.storyText:
Hey HN!

I shared Optio here back in March. Originally it was focused on getting swarms of coding agents (claude code/codex) to drive PRs towards a merge by automatically resuming them on CI failures or PR comments.

Since then, I've reworked the project to be a general platform for running any kind of AI workflow on your infra by allowing users to configure each component of a possible workflow:

When: On demand, a cron schedule, or triggered by external events such as a webhook, slack message, ticket (jira/linear/gh), pagerduty/datadog/alertsmanager/pylon/sentry.

Where: In a k8s pod or any machine you have installed the optio daemon on (I use my laptop).

Who: Any harness you prefer (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, etc.)

What/Why: You can format parameters from the triggers directly into the prompts and then configure if the agent should exit, be resumed automatically, or be persistent.

You can either define workflows in the web ui or as yaml files that get synced to the orchestrator (ai config-as-code).

I've also built native iOS and Android apps so you can connect to your cluster and create/manage agents remotely.

The marketing page is at https://optio.host and the code is still open source at https://github.com/jonwiggins/optio

Would love feedback or any thoughts you might have on how I could make it better!
